Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")

tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported

# Probe helper: runs the original ./executable in an isolated dstask repo.

14 15 Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to 16 [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of 17 a special protocol. 18 19 If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge 20 conflict, then dstask is for you! 21 22 https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc 23 24 [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) 25 26 ## Features 27 28 - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) 29 - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! 30 - Task listing won't break with long task text 31 - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** 32 - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser 33 - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows 34 - A single statically-linked binary 35 - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. 36 37 ## Non-features 38 39 - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for 40 projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial 41 to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a 42 multi-person project tracked elsewhere. 43 44 ## Requirements 45 46 - Git 47 - A 256-color capable terminal 48 49 ## Installation 50 51 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. 52 - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). 53 - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 54 1. Enable shell completions: 55 - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. 56 - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. 57 - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 58 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 59 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: 60 - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` 61 - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` 62 63 ## PowerShell completion 64 65 Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: 66 67 ```powershell 68 dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 69 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' 70 ``` 71 72 ## Usage 73 74 Run `dstask help` for usage information. 75 76 ### Basic Commands 77 78 - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task 79 - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on 80 - `dstask start` - Start working on a task 81 - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task 82 - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete 83 - `dstask edit` - Edit a task 84 - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task 85 - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note 86 - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks 87 - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks 88 - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks 89 - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) 90 - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote 91 92 ### Task Properties 93 94 - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) 95 - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` 96 - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` 97 - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` 98 - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved 99 100 ### Contexts 101 102 Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: 103 104 ```bash 105 dstask context work 106 dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work 107 dstask # shows only work tasks 108 dstask context -- # clear context 109 ``` 110 111 ### Git Sync 112 113 Sync your tasks across devices using git: 114 115 ```bash 116 # Set up sync on first device 117 cd ~/.dstask 118 git remote add origin 119 git push -u origin master 120 121 # On other devices 122 git clone ~/.dstask 123 124 # To sync 125 dstask sync 126 ``` 127 128 ### Templates 129 130 Create task templates for recurring patterns: 131 132 ```bash 133 dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 134 dstask add from-template 135 ``` 136 137 ## Best Practices 138 139 - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. 140 - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. 141 - Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context. 142 - Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately. 143 - Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this. 144 - Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top. 145 - Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up. 146 - Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks 147 - Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task 148 - Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly! 149 - set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. With direnv, this allows you to automatically switch context 150 151 ## Database 152 153 The default database location is: 154 155 - Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/` 156 - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask` 157 158 It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`. 159 160 ## Integration of fuzzy finders 161 162 Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to 163 search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell 164 wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: 165 166 ```bash 167 function dstask () { 168 local has_double_dash subcommand 169 170 if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then 171 has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" 172 subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" 173 if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ 174 [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] 175 then 176 command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ 177 | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ 178 | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ 179 | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" 180 return 181 fi 182 fi 183 184 command dstask "$@" 185 } 186 ``` 187 188 The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` 189 command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All 190 other commands are passed directly to dstask. 191 192 ## Alternatives 193 194 Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. 195 196 - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell 197 - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue 198 - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support 199 - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) 200 - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager 201 - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy 202 203 ## FAQ 204 205 > Does dstask encrypt tasks? 206 207 Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. If you want to have your remote 208 repository encrypted, you may consider 209 [git-remote-gcrypt](https://spwhitton.name/tech/code/git-remote-gcrypt/) or 210 [git-crypt](https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt). Note that dstask has not been 211 tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the 212 tools themselves. 213 214 > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? 215 216 Yes. 217 218 1. Set a context: 219 2. Run a modify command without and ID 220 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context 221 222 This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before 223 modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of 224 potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. 225 226 You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. 227 228 > Is there a GUI or web interface? 229 230 Not as part of dstask itself. Probed binary: `/workspace/executable` (dstask, `version` prints "Unknown"). All experiments via

## 1. Output mode selection

- stdout NOT a TTY → **JSON array on stdout**, nothing else, no trailing newline (output ends with `]`).
- stdout IS a TTY (or `DSTASK_FAKE_PTY` set to **any value, even `0`/`yes`**) → colored table rendering.
- `DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1` simulates a fixed **80 columns x 24 rows** terminal. `COLUMNS`/`LINES` env are ignored.
- Real TTY: geometry comes from **ioctl (TIOCGWINSZ)** (`stty cols/rows` changes it); `COLUMNS`/`LINES` env are ignored.
  Degenerate case: when ioctl reports width 0 (e.g. `script -qec` with no winsize), rows render as ~13-17
  padding spaces with no visible text (buggy edge case).
- Listing commands never invoke git; stderr is empty on success in both modes.
- Bare `dstask` == `dstask next` in every respect (byte-identical JSON and TTY output).
- `next` and `show-open` produce **identical** output except: in TTY mode `next` truncates the number of
  rows to fit the terminal height, `show-open` never truncates. In piped/JSON mode they are byte-identical
  (no truncation ever).

## 2. JSON output (piped mode) — all listing commands

- 2-space indented JSON array, exact key set and order for every command
  (`next`, bare, `show-open`, `show-active`, `show-paused`, `show-resolved`, `show-templates`, `show-unorganised`):

```
uuid, status, id, summary, notes, tags, project, priority, created, resolved, due
```

- No `subtasks`, `dependencies`, `delegatedto` fields in JSON (they exist in on-disk YAML but are omitted).
- `notes` IS included, full text with `\n` escapes.
- Field formats:

  - `tags`: array (alphabetical; `[]` when none). `project`: string (`""` when none). `priority`: `"P0".."P3"`.

  - unset time = Go zero time: `"0001-01-01T00:00:00Z"`.
- Empty result → `[]` (exactly two bytes, no newline), exit code 0.
- No "N tasks." line, no "Active context:" line, no critical-task warning in JSON mode — pure JSON only.

- **Always outputs the piped-style JSON array, even on a TTY** (with FAKE_PTY too). No table, no count
  line, no "Active context:" line, no critical warning. Exit 0; empty → `[]`.
- Help: `Usage: dstask resolved` / "Show a report of last 1000 resolved tasks." (1000-cap not tested).
- Sorted by `resolved` ascending. All resolved tasks have `"id": 0`.
- Respects the active context (filtered) and filter args; `--` bypasses context.

## 9. Context behavior

Set with `dstask context +work` (stored in `<repo>/.git/dstask/state.bin`; ids in `ids.bin`).

- With a context active, TTY table AND single-view modes print a first line:
  `ESC[33mActive context: +workESC[0m` (yellow, SGR 33). NOT printed in JSON mode, NOT printed by
  `show-resolved` (JSON), NOT printed when `--` is given.
- `next`/bare and `show-open`: context ANDs with any filter args.
- `show-active`, `show-paused`, `show-templates`, `show-resolved`: all filtered by context too.
- `show-unorganised`: **ignores the context entirely** ("global context" per help) — but still prints the
  `Active context: +work` line in TTY mode.
- `--` bypasses the context and works in any position (`dstask -- next`, `dstask next --`,
  `dstask next -- +home` all equivalent).
- Context `none` clears it (`dstask context none`).

## 10. Filter arguments (after the command)

- `+tag` require tag, `-tag` exclude tag; multiple tags AND (`+home +work` → must have both).
- `project:name` require project; `P0`..`P3` require exact priority.
- Bare words: **all words joined with spaces into one phrase**, matched as a **case-insensitive substring
  against summary + notes**. `next critical bug` matches "fix critical bug in parser"; `next bug critical`
  matches nothing; `next CRITICAL` matches. A word appearing only in notes matches.
- All filter terms AND together. Empty result rules per section 7.

- Printed on stdout after the listing when ≥1 open **P0** task is excluded from the current view:

  tasks elsewhere prints `3 critical task(s)...`; full `next` containing all P0s prints nothing).
- Appears in table mode directly after the `N tasks.` line; in single-view after the detail block (and after
  the notes block's trailing blank line when notes exist). Always literal `task(s)`.
- Not printed in JSON mode.

## 12. Task IDs (observed, relevant to `id` field)

- IDs are small ints assigned at add time as the **lowest free positive integer**, sticky per task
  (persisted in `.git/dstask/ids.bin`). Resolving a task frees its id; the next added task reuses it
  (verified: id 7 freed by `done`, reused by a later `add`).

Notes written to `/workspace/notes/02-list.md` (290 lines, with verbatim `cat -A` captures). Key findings:

- **Two output modes**: piped → pure JSON array (no trailing newline, `[]` when empty, exit 0 always); TTY → colored tables. `DSTASK_FAKE_PTY` with ANY value (even `0`) forces TTY mode at a fixed **80x24** geometry; real TTYs use ioctl (`stty cols/rows`), and `COLUMNS`/`LINES` env are always ignored.
- **JSON schema is identical for all 8 commands**: exactly 11 keys in fixed order `uuid,status,id,summary,notes,tags,project,priority,created,resolved,due`. Notes included; subtasks/dependencies/delegatedto omitted. Resolved tasks always report `"id": 0`. Timestamps are RFC3339-nano with variable fractional digits; unset = `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`.
- **`next` == bare `dstask` == `show-open`** except: TTY `next` caps rows at `max(8, termRows-9)` (15 under FAKE_PTY) and prints `15/60 tasks shown.`; `show-open` never truncates. Summary cells hard-truncate to width in both.
- **Sorting**: priority (P0→P3), then `created` ascending — status/ID/overdue don't affect order. `show-resolved` sorts by `resolved` ascending.
- **Surprise 1**: `show-resolved` prints JSON even on a TTY — no table ever.
- **Surprise 2**: exactly-one-match renders a Name/Value detail view (rows: ID, Priority, Summary, Status, Project, Tags, UUID, Created, Due-if-set), plus a grey `Notes on task N:` block; no count line.
- **Surprise 3**: TTY listings print a red `N critical task(s) outside this context! Use \`dstask -- P0\`...` warning counting P0 tasks excluded from the current view — even with no context set.
- Row colors: zebra bg 232/233, fg by priority (160/166/250/245); **overdue or due-today promotes fg to 166** (P0 stays 160); paused bg 236; active bg 250 with dark fg (P0=124, P1=130, P2=233, P3=238).
- Empty repo → `No tasks found. Run \`dstask help\`...` exit 0; tasks exist but filter excludes all → stderr red `No matching tasks in given context or filter.`, exit **1** (TTY only; piped stays `[]`/exit 0).
- Context: yellow `Active context: +work` line in TTY; all commands respect it except `show-unorganised` (global, per docs) — `--` bypasses in any position. Filters: words join into one phrase, case-insensitive substring over summary+notes; `+tag`/`-tag`/`project:`/`Pn` AND together.
- Due rendering: `today`/`tomorrow`/`Mon 10`/`17 Aug`/`1 Jan 2020`. IDs are sticky, lowest-free (freed ids get reused). Subtask YAML parses only as a list of `{uuid:}` maps; no CLI way found to create them.
